title: One-pass greedy
sub: The minimum so far, the farthest reachable point, and Kadane: "extend or start over"
cards/0/title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock: what you need from the past at step j
cards/0/body:
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (LeetCode #121). prices[i] is the price on day i. Buy once and sell on one of the later days; find the largest profit, or 0 if no profit is possible. n ≤ 10⁵, prices up to 10⁴. Example: [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4] → 5: buy at 1, sell at 6.

Naively you try every pair "buy on i, sell on j > i": O(n²), about 5·10⁹ for n = 10⁵ — too slow.

The question that unlocks one-pass greedy: what do I actually need from the past at step j? To sell on day j you do not need the whole history, just one number — the lowest price before j. If the past boils down to one or two numbers (a minimum, a maximum, the farthest point), you update them on the fly, and the solution is O(n) time and O(1) memory.

Signals in the problem: the answer is built from pairs i < j or from a prefix, the order of elements is fixed (days, indices), and "the best so far" does not depend on what comes later.
cards/1/q: In which problems is everything you need from the past just one or two numbers updated on the fly? Select all that apply.
cards/1/options/0: The largest difference a[j] − a[i] with i < j
cards/1/options/1: Whether the array contains two equal numbers
cards/1/options/2: The largest health drawdown: the peak so far minus the current value
cards/1/options/3: How many times each word of a text occurs
cards/1/options/4: The second largest element of an array
cards/1/explain: The difference is the stock problem again: the minimum so far. The drawdown is the mirror image: the maximum so far minus the current value. The second largest is two numbers, the first and second maximum. Duplicates and word counts cannot be reduced to a couple of numbers: you have to remember everything seen — a set or a dictionary from the hash table unit.
cards/2/title: The idea: the minimum so far
cards/2/body:
Walk the days keeping two numbers. minPrice is the lowest price among the days seen: the best buy day for any sale from now on. best is the best profit among the sales that could already have happened.

Invariant: after step j, minPrice = min(prices[0..j]) and best is the maximum of prices[b] − prices[a] over all a ≤ b ≤ j. A new day either updates the minimum or yields a candidate p − minPrice.

A new minimum does not reset best: the earlier deal is already counted, and the minimum only serves future sales. The order of the two lines in the loop does not affect the answer: if you update the minimum first, selling on the same day gives 0, which does not spoil the maximum.

In a game: telemetry — the largest FPS drop from a previous peak (maximum so far), or the largest rating gain between two matches (minimum so far). One pass over the history, no pairs.
cards/2/deep:
It is Kadane on differences. Let d[i] = prices[i] − prices[i − 1]. The profit from buying at a and selling at b is the sum of d[a + 1..b], a subarray of differences. The maximum profit is the maximum subarray sum of d (or 0). Kadane's algorithm is further on in this lesson.

The proof in one sentence. The optimal deal (a, b) is considered at step b: by then minPrice ≤ prices[a], so the candidate prices[b] − minPrice is at least the optimum, and it cannot exceed the optimum because it is a real deal too.

int.MaxValue as the start. The first price is bound to become the minimum, and an empty array returns 0 without a separate branch. p − minPrice cannot overflow: by then minPrice is no greater than p.
cards/3/explain: The minimum starts at int.MaxValue so the first price replaces it right away; starting at 0 it would never update. The minimum is Math.Min, the profit is sale minus purchase: p − minPrice. Starting at int.MinValue would break the minimum, and minPrice − p is a loss.
cards/4/task: Step through the trace on [4, 9, 2, 8, 1, 5]. The rig stops twice and asks what the code will do on the next day. Watch two numbers: the minimum so far and the best profit.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: best resets to 0: the old purchase no longer counts
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: minPrice stays 4: you must buy before the best sale
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: Days 0 and 1 are done: minPrice = 4, best = 5 (buy at 4, sell at 9). Day 2, price 2. What does the code do?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: Two is a new minimum: the best purchase for every future sale. The profit of 5 is already earned and stays in best. The minimum serves the future and best records the past, so neither resets the other.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: Day 3, price 8. minPrice = 2, best = 5. What does the code do?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: A sale on day 3 is compared with the cheapest day before it — that is 2, not 4. 8 − 2 = 6 > 5 — a new best. 9 − 2 is not a deal: the nine came before the two, and you cannot sell before you buy. Later the minimum becomes 1, but 5 − 1 = 4 does not beat the record: the answer is 6.
cards/5/title: Jump Game (#55): the farthest reachable point
cards/5/body:
The problem. nums[i] is the longest jump from cell i (you may jump any distance from 1 to nums[i]). You start at 0. Can you reach the last cell? n ≤ 10⁴.

Naively you mark reachable cells: from every reachable i, mark i + 1 … i + nums[i]. That is O(n²): each cell may mark up to n neighbours.

The observation: the set of reachable cells is always a range [0, reach]. If you can jump to j, you can also land on any cell in between: a jump can be any length up to the maximum. So one number is enough — reach, the farthest reachable cell.

Invariant: before step i, all cells 0..reach are reachable and nothing beyond is. If i > reach, cell i cannot be reached, nor can anything to its right: the answer is false. Otherwise reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]). A zero in nums[i] is dangerous only if reach sits exactly on it: a zero inside the range is jumped over.

In a game: validating a procedurally generated corridor level where each point has its own dash range — can the level be completed? One pass instead of a path search.
cards/6/task: Step through the trace on [3, 2, 1, 0, 4]. There is a long jump at the end of the array, but the rig will stop and ask whether the code ever gets to it.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: It skips i = 4 and returns true at the end of the loop
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: Cells 0–3 are done, reach = 3 — exactly on cell 3 with its zero, not beyond it. Next is i = 4, nums[4] = 4. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: Each of the cells 0–3 reaches exactly 3: 0 + 3, 1 + 2, 2 + 1, 3 + 0. The four in nums[4] would jump to the end, but you cannot get into cell 4 itself: i > reach. The trap is a zero sitting exactly on the reach boundary: there is nothing to jump over it with. A zero left of the boundary would be harmless.
cards/7/body:
Maximum Subarray (#53). The largest sum of a non-empty subarray. n ≤ 10⁵, numbers from −10⁴ to 10⁴. Trying all subarrays with prefix sums is O(n²), about 5·10⁹.

The idea. Ask for each position i: what is the best sum of a subarray that ends exactly at i? There are two options: extend the best one ending at i − 1, or start over with nums[i] alone. cur = max(nums[i], cur + nums[i]): if the running sum is negative, it only drags you down — better to start fresh. The answer is the maximum of cur over all i.

This is dynamic programming with a single cell: dp[i] = max(nums[i], dp[i − 1] + nums[i]), and only the last dp is needed — the array collapses into a variable. Dynamic programming is covered in depth in the backtracking and DP unit.

Start from nums[0], not 0: the subarray is non-empty, and in an all-negative array the answer is the largest of them. No overflow: |sum| ≤ 10⁵ · 10⁴ = 10⁹. In a game: the luckiest stretch of a run, when each round has a known income minus spending. The rig runs it next.
cards/7/deep:
Why it is correct. The best subarray ending at i is either nums[i] alone, or the best subarray ending at i − 1 plus nums[i]: if some non-best subarray ended at i − 1, swapping in the best one would not decrease the sum. That gives the recurrence, and the global answer is the maximum over all ends.

The subarray bounds. Remember the start whenever cur starts over (nums[i] > cur + nums[i], i.e. cur < 0), and copy the pair "start, i" whenever best improves.

Other solutions. Divide and conquer gives O(n log n) and sometimes comes up as a follow-up: "now without Kadane". Through prefix sums: max(P[j] − min P[i < j]) — the stock problem again, just on prefixes. All three are the same thing: "the best so far" in one number.
cards/8/task: Step through Kadane on [2, −5, 3, −1, 4, −10, 2]. The rig stops twice and asks whether the code extends the run or starts over. Watch two numbers: cur and best.
cards/8/goal/asks/0/q: i = 2, x = 3, cur = −3, best = 2. What does the code do?
cards/8/goal/asks/0/explain: cur = max(x, cur + x) = max(3, 0) = 3. The running sum −3 is negative and only drags down: a subarray ending at i = 2 is better off starting at x itself. The run is now [3], and best becomes 3 right away.
cards/8/goal/asks/1/q: i = 5, x = −10, cur = 6, best = 6. What does the code do?
cards/8/goal/asks/1/explain: max(−10, 6 − 10) = −4: extending still beats starting at −10 — the comparison is with x alone, not with zero. cur falls to −4, but best remembers 6: the answer is the maximum over the whole pass, not the last cur. On the next step the negative cur loses to x = 2 and the code starts over — but best no longer changes.
cards/9/q: On [-3, -1, -2] this code returns 0, but the answer is −1. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/9/explain: Math.Max(0, …) allows an empty subarray with sum 0, while the problem requires a non-empty one. On all-negative input cur becomes 0 every time, and best = 0. Starting over means starting from x itself: cur = Math.Max(x, cur + x). Then cur = 0 at the start is harmless: the first step gives max(x, x) = x.
cards/10/title: Variations: what else one pass solves
cards/10/body:
Stock with unlimited deals (#122). You may buy and sell any number of times, holding at most one share. The answer is the sum of all rises: every prices[i] − prices[i − 1] > 0 is a separate deal. A long rise over several days gives the same total as one deal from the bottom to the peak.

Jump Game II (#45). Reaching the end is guaranteed — find the minimum number of jumps. Greedy by "layers": curEnd is the boundary of cells reachable with the current number of jumps, farthest is how far you can get from them. When you reach curEnd, the layer is over: one more jump, and the new boundary is farthest. It is a breadth-first search without a queue, O(n).

Maximum product subarray (#152). Minus times minus is plus, so you keep two numbers ending at i: the maximum and the minimum. A negative nums[i] swaps their roles.

A circular array (#918). The best subarray either does not wrap around — plain Kadane — or it does, and then it is "everything minus the worst subarray": total − minSub. The exception is an all-negative array: there total − minSub corresponds to an empty subarray, and the answer is plain Kadane.
cards/10/deep:
Why layers give the minimum. The cells reachable in at most k jumps form a range starting at 0 (for the same reason as in Jump Game), and the next layer extends it up to farthest. It is a breadth-first search on the graph "cell → cells a jump can land on", where the layers are ranges, so no queue is needed. The loop runs to n − 2: there is no need to jump from the last cell.

When one pass is not enough. Stocks with a fee, with a one-day "cooldown" after selling, or with at most k deals involve several states: "holding a share" and "not holding" (and the deal number). That is DP over states, waiting in the DP unit. The sign: the answer at step i depends not on a single "best so far" but on which state you arrived in.
cards/11/q: Maximum Subarray in an interview, out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: is the subarray non-empty? What are n and the values, is int enough?
cards/11/items/1: Naive: all subarrays via prefix sums — O(n²)
cards/11/items/2: The idea: the best sum ending at i — extend the previous one or start over
cards/11/items/3: Code with the invariant: cur is the best sum ending at i, best is the best overall
cards/11/items/6: Edge cases: all negative, one element, sum overflow
cards/11/explain: The question "is the subarray non-empty" at the start directly determines how cur and best start: nums[0], not 0. The "all negative" edge case at the end checks exactly that.
cards/12/q: Match the problem with what you keep in one pass.
